**By Roger Hancock, CEO of Recall InfoLink**

I've been watching this summer's Cyclospora outbreak the way I watch every recall, which is closely and with a fair amount of frustration.

Consumers have been asking reasonable questions for weeks. Why did so many people have to get sick before anyone decided to recall anything? Once the recall was issued, why did it seem to do so little to stop people from getting sick? If this is a predictable food safety event, one that arrives every summer, why wasn't the supply chain ready to move faster? Why wasn’t it prevented in the first place, and why has this year been worse instead of better? This is more than I can unpack in a short op-ed, but there are a few things I can offer from the recall side that may help address the confusion that has been so rampant.

Let’s start with what was hard about this recall, because some of it was justifiably complicated. Cyclospora is difficult to detect in food, which is why a sample read positive on July 18 and was called a false positive a day later. Symptoms take about a week to appear, sometimes two, so investigators were asking sick people across multiple states to reconstruct meals from ten days back and find the overlap. Lab results take time, and early information often gets revised. Supply chains cross international borders, which means different compliance requirements, and more complicated traceback pathways. Some of this is unavoidable, some of it could be improved drastically. Still, we’ll never get away from complicated recalls.

title: New Zealand and French studies call attention to Campylobacter
summary:
A study in New Zealand has provided an insight into Campylobacter contamination and antimicrobial resistance in fresh chicken.

Campylobacter was detected in 50 percent of 24 samples. Among confirmed isolates, there were high levels of resistance to tetracycline and ciprofloxacin, while the majority were susceptible to erythromycin.

title: Public health officials investigating Salmonella outbreak in Utah
summary:

The department says it is actively investigating the source of the illness and taking steps to limit further spread.
